pageProps.body:
🗣️ Cantonese Under Pressure

Related: Home | Glory to Hong Kong | Book Censorship under the NSL | Press Freedom under Siege

Cantonese (粵語 / 廣東話) is the everyday tongue of the overwhelming majority of Hongkongers — the language of its streets and wet markets, its cinema and Canto-pop, its courtrooms, its classrooms and its protests. By the 2021 census, over 88% of residents speak Cantonese as their usual language and close to 94% can speak it (HKFP). And yet, again and again, the institutions that govern the city have treated it as negotiable — a "dialect," a thing to be set aside as Mandarin rises. This collection tracks that slow squeeze, and the people who refuse to let the mother tongue go quiet.

A language, not a "dialect"

Whether Cantonese is a "language" or a mere "dialect" of Chinese is, for Hongkongers, a question of identity as much as linguistics — and the answer carries political weight. If Cantonese is "just" a dialect, its exclusion from education and officialdom might be waved through; if it is a language in its own right, favouring Putonghua at its expense "smacks of politics."

By the linguists' test — mutual comprehensibility — Cantonese is not a dialect of Mandarin: the two are about as different as two Romance languages, and Cantonese is spoken by roughly as many people as Italian. As the oft-quoted line attributed to linguist Max Weinreich has it, "a language is a dialect with an army and a navy." Cantonese also carries a longer literary lineage than Putonghua — the SCMP columnist Alex Lo notes it may trace to Tang-dynasty speech, citing the scholar Nan Huai-chin that "Hakka and Cantonese were the Tang dynasty's national languages… Putonghua is a [recent] national language" (China Digital Times).

When institutions treat the mother tongue as optional

2014 — "a Chinese dialect that is not an official language"

In January 2014, the Education Bureau posted an article on its Language Learning Support page that, while promoting bilingualism and trilingualism as the city "develops alongside the rapidly growing China," stated: "Although the Basic Law stipulates that Chinese and English are the two official languages in Hong Kong, nearly 97 per cent of the local population learn Cantonese (a Chinese dialect that is not an official language) as their commonly used daily language."

The line drew a storm of criticism. The Basic Law names "Chinese" and English as official languages but defines no spoken standard; as Eric Cheung Tat-ming, principal law lecturer at the University of Hong Kong, pointed out, "there have never been attempts to define what official languages mean in the oral context," and in Hong Kong's courts and official settings "the choice of the spoken language has been one based on commonality, so Cantonese is preferred." Within days the Education Bureau deleted the article (China Digital Times · SCMP).

2026 — a school brands Cantonese "strictly forbidden"

On 22 September 2026, the prestigious girls' school Good Hope School (德望學校) issued a full withdrawal of a graduation-video production guideline that had declared Cantonese "STRICTLY FORBIDDEN" for speech, dialogue and voiceovers — students "must use English or Mandarin." Screenshots of the guideline had gone viral on Threads over the weekend.

Reversing course, the school said it bore "full responsibility," that language "carries our memories, emotions, affections and is the living soul of our heritage," and that it had "never been our ethos to constrain the mother tongue of any child entrusted to our care." Principal Gary Harfitt apologised, calling the slide an unrevised draft that did not reflect school policy — though the statement did not explain why the guideline had been issued. The Education Bureau said it had urged the school to review its event arrangements but declined to comment on the school's language policy (HKFP).

A fight over the classroom — in tongue and in content

The squeeze on Cantonese is one front in a longer contest over what Hong Kong's children learn, and in whose language. The other front is content. In 2012, the student group Scholarism, led by a 15-year-old Joshua Wong, drove the movement that forced the government to shelve a compulsory "Moral and National Education" curriculum critics condemned as "brainwashing"; the protests drew more than 100,000 people and launched a generation of student activism (CNN). Scholarism did not campaign on Cantonese as such — but defending the mother tongue and resisting a Beijing-centred syllabus spring from the same anxiety, the mainlandisation of Hong Kong's schools, which is why the Education Bureau's 2014 "not an official language" remark landed so hard in that already-charged period.

Keeping Cantonese alive

The pressure on Cantonese is rarely a ban; more often it is a quiet reweighting — Mandarin framed as the language of the future, Cantonese as sentiment. But the mother tongue has proved stubborn. It remains the voice of Hong Kong's culture and of its civic life: the protest anthem Glory to Hong Kong was written and sung in Cantonese, and Cantonese-language journalism and film (see Hong Kong protest films) keep the idiom in the public record. Among the diaspora, Cantonese classes, reading groups and recordings have become a form of preservation in themselves.

This page is an early, growing hub. Still to be documented: the Putonghua-medium-of-instruction debate in schools, Cantonese in broadcasting and government, and the diaspora's preservation efforts. See the tracking issue #33.

Help preserve Cantonese

Cantonese lives in use. If you have material worth keeping — oral histories, classroom or teaching materials, recordings, screenshots of language policies, or your own account of where Cantonese has been pushed out or defended — you can contribute through our submission channels. Small, specific records are welcome.

Sources

  • HKFP: Prestigious Hong Kong school withdraws unapproved Cantonese ban following controversy (22 Sept 2026)
  • China Digital Times: Is Cantonese a Dialect or a Language? (18 Feb 2014)
  • SCMP: Education Bureau rapped over Cantonese 'not an official language' gaffe (2014)
  • CNN: 'National education' raises furor in Hong Kong (30 July 2012)

[![Great Extinction](/assets/extinctions.jpeg)](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/) 
> (_Courtesy: [Hong Kong Freepress](https://hongkongfp.com/2021/11/28/explainer-over-50-groups-gone-in-11-months-how-hong-kongs-pro-democracy-forces-crumbled/), 2021_) 

SHKO (Save Hong Kong Online) is a community-driven project dedicated to preserving the rapidly disappearing websites and online resources of Hong Kong’s civil society and independent media since 2019. In response to the sweeping shutdowns caused by political changes in Hong Kong, we aim to safeguard digital heritage before it vanishes. This project is anonymous, open source, and supported by a global network of contributors.

While most sites in our archive were forced offline due to Hong Kong’s political deterioration, it’s important to note that [[RFA Cantonese|sites.rfa_cantonese]] is the only site here closed not because of Hong Kong’s situation, but due to internal political decisions in the United States.

Explore our full list of preserved sites and archives on the [Collections page](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/).

Recent work: documenting the [[Hong Kong Fire 2025|hong-kong-fire-2025]] tragedy at Wang Fuk Court (168 dead, ongoing probes into flammable mesh/foam, bid-rigging, and a judge-led review), including activism, timeline, and investigation subpages; and the [[⚖️ Jimmy Lai case|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]] — Apple Daily founder sentenced to 20 years under the National Security Law (Feb 2026), with coverage of press freedom impact and international response; and [[🎵 Glory to Hong Kong|glory-to-hong-kong]] — the 2019 protest anthem and the 2024 court order that made it the first song banned in Hong Kong since the 1997 handover; and [[📕 Book Censorship under the NSL|book-censorship]] — how Hong Kong criminalised the printed word, from the banned Sheep Village children's-book trilogy (whose speech-therapist authors were jailed for sedition) and purged public libraries to the 2026 bookshop raids; and [[🗽 Statues & Monuments|statues]] — how Hong Kong's public monuments to Tiananmen and the 2019 protests (the Pillar of Shame, the Goddess of Democracy, Lady Liberty) were removed, seized as police evidence, and driven into exile abroad; and [[⚖️ The Hong Kong 47|hong-kong-47]] — the largest National Security Law case, in which 45 pro-democracy figures were jailed for up to 10 years over a 2020 opposition primary election; and [[🕯️ Tiananmen Vigil|tiananmen-vigil]] — the thirty-year Victoria Park candlelight vigil for the 1989 crackdown, the largest June 4th commemoration on Chinese soil, now banned and its organisers jailed; and [[✊ Faces of the Crackdown|faces-of-the-crackdown]] — a human index to the publishers, students, unionists and clergy jailed, exiled or tried under the National Security Law; and [[🎬 Films & Documentaries|films]] — the protest movement on film, a decade of documentaries and features (Ten Years, Revolution of Our Times, the Joshua Wong doc) now largely banned or unshowable in Hong Kong, gathered with their trailers; and [[📰 Press Freedom under Siege|press-freedom]] — how one of Asia's freest presses was dismantled in five years, from the raids that closed Apple Daily and Stand News to the revived sedition law now reaching lone online reporters; and [[🗣️ Cantonese Under Pressure|cantonese]] — how Hong Kong's mother tongue, spoken by nearly everyone yet official to no one, is squeezed in schools and officialdom, from the Education Bureau's 2014 "not an official language" gaffe to a prestigious school's 2026 attempt to forbid Cantonese in a graduation video; and [[🖼️ Culture Under Control|culture-under-control]] — how Hong Kong's flagship cultural institutions, above all the M+ museum, quietly police their own programmes under the National Security Law, from Ai Weiwei's withheld Tiananmen photograph at the 2021 opening to the 2026 cancellation of a Hou Hsiao-hsien classic for unexplained "technical reasons."

## Goals
- To preserve as much information as possible before its disappearance during Hong Kong's great transition
- To illustrate a viable method that everyone can use to help preserve online heritage with no pains
- To demonstrate global collaborations to save local digital heritages with best practices

## Quick Facts

We are working on over dozens of [[websites or online causes | sites]] in Hong Kong in the past two decades which has been forced to shutdown or at the brink of disappearing. We'd welcome anyone help [[contribute | participation]] to the content and/or [[sponsor | sponsorship]] our program to sustain it together. 

Examples:
- [[sites.appledaily]] (Extincted)
- [[sites.inmediahk]] (In Danger)
